Foreword from the Vice-Chancellor [PERSON] Plan articulates the direction of the [ORGANISATION] across the period 2026 to 2031, under conditions that are, by deliberate institutional choice, more sharply specified than the conditions assumed in any of the University’s recent strategic plans. The working assumption is set out plainly below; each subsequent commitment in the Plan can be read against it. Working assumption. By 2029, general-purpose artificial intelligence systems will be performing the great majority of cognitive labour currently undertaken by university administrators, academic staff, and graduates of the University, at or above the standard of competent professional practice. The University accepts this working assumption as the operating context for the present Plan and will reshape itself accordingly. The University has, across the working group’s deliberations, taken the view that an institution of [ORGANISATION]’s standing has a particular responsibility under these conditions: —4—

not merely to adapt operationally to the foreseeable changes, but to lead the country’s intellectual and civic preparation for them. The Plan accordingly addresses both the internal reshaping of the institution and the University’s contribution to the broader national settlement that the working group considers, on the balance of available evidence, very likely to be required.

We are aware that the working assumption may strike some readers as overconfident. The working group considered the alternative assumptions across many weeks of consultation and concluded that the asymmetry of consequences favours acting on the assumption that proves substantially correct, rather than maintaining the assumption that proves comfortably wrong. A national research university that prepares for the conditions described in this Plan and finds them delayed by five years will have lost relatively little. A national research university that prepares for the conditions of the previous decade and finds them transformed by the conditions described in this Plan will, by 2031, no longer be the institution the country requires it to be. The Plan is commended to the community as a structural response to a structural moment. Vice-Chancellor and President

The third signal is the country’s collective unpreparedness. The working group has consulted with senior figures across the public service, the political class, and civil society and has come to the view that the country does not yet have a settled framework for the social, economic, and democratic consequences of the working assumption. The University considers itself uniquely placed to contribute to that framework. The fourth signal is the rate at which graduate destinations are already shifting. The early cohorts entering the workforce in 2025 and 2026 are encountering professional conditions different in kind, not merely in degree, from the conditions their immediate predecessors encountered. The working group has examined the destination data across the previous three undergraduate cohorts and has concluded that the trend is consistent with the working assumption. Read together, these four signals ask the University to articulate a posture that is structurally responsive to the moment. The posture this Plan adopts is, by deliberate institutional choice, more sharply specified than the postures of recent strategic plans. The University is acting on the working assumption, not waiting for it to be confirmed.

Our ambition By 2031, [ORGANISATION] will be a university that has, over the run of this Plan, structurally reshaped itself in light of the working assumption and made a substantive contribution to the country’s preparation for the conditions the working assumption describes. The University will have wound down those of its functions whose continuation is no longer defensible, cultivated the institutional and civic vocations the working group considers least automatable, and contributed visibly to the democratic shaping of the post-cognitive-labour settlement. The University will be smaller in some dimensions and larger in others. It will, by 2031, be the institution the country requires it to be in the conditions the country will, by then, be operating in.

Strategic priorities The Three-Year Horizon and the Wind-Down of Cognitive Labour Premise. The working assumption set out in the foreword has particular implications for those institutional functions whose continuation, on the working assumption, is no longer defensible. The Plan addresses those functions honestly, in the conviction that a national research university owes the staff, students, and country it serves a structured, dignified, and well-supported wind-down rather than a gradual erosion under conditions of denial. Initiatives. 1. Establish the AI Transition Office, chaired by a Deputy Vice-Chancellor and reporting directly to Council, charged with identifying institutional functions for structured wind-down and supporting the people whose work the wind-down affects. 2. Publish, by the end of 2026, an Honesty Statement on the AI Transition, addressed to current students and reviewed annually, setting out the working group’s best assessment of the conditions graduates of each degree will encounter on entering the workforce. 3. Convene a quarterly Three-Year Horizon Review, chaired by the Vice-Chancellor and attended by the Deputy Vice-Chancellors, examining the current state of the working assumption and the University’s structural response. Measures. 1. By the end of 2026, the Honesty Statement on the AI Transition will have been published and made accessible to every current student of the University. 2. By 2029, the AI Transition Office will have completed structured wind-down assessments of every institutional function nominated for review by the Three year Horizon Review.

Custodianship of the Last Human Vocations Premise. The working assumption does not bear uniformly across the institution’s functions. Several vocations — pastoral, contemplative, ceremonial, embodied, and place-based — are considered by the working group to be substantially less automatable across the plan period. The University proposes to identify, protect, and patiently cultivate these vocations as a substantive institutional commitment. Initiatives.

How we developed this plan This Plan was developed over fourteen months through a process of facilitated consultation across staff, students, alumni, partners, the [PERSON] Family Trust, and the country’s principal [PERSON] scholars. The [PERSON] Family Trust contributed substantively to the working group’s deliberations about the centenary programme and to the preservation arrangements for the archive. The working group also consulted with the curators of the Questacon [PERSON] exhibition (2013) and with the producers of the 2014 ABC documentary series in order to draw on the existing public-facing scholarship. The framing language of the Plan — “the [PERSON] disposition”, “the patient examination of the half-baked”, “the tartan paint line item” — emerged from the consultation rather than being imposed at the outset. Where the language has been retained, it is because participants in the working group returned to it spontaneously across multiple rounds.

Chancellor remains accountable to Council for delivery. Within that frame, three governance moves give the Plan effective traction. First, a [PERSON] Centenary Standing Committee, chaired by a Deputy Vice-Chancellor and reporting quarterly to Council, takes responsibility for the indicator set across all four priorities and for ensuring that the centenary year in 2031 finds the University in the institutional condition the tradition warrants. Second, an Accountability and Review schedule, published annually, sets out which indicators are due for full reporting in which quarter, with no indicator permitted to slip beyond the next quarterly review cycle. Third, Council’s Audit and Risk Committee will, from 2027, treat indicator slippage on the same footing as financial sustainability. Annual reporting against the Plan will be published in full, including instances of indicator slippage, elements of the Plan that have not progressed at the pace this document anticipated, and any element of the [PERSON] Centenary Programme that has been reprioritised or deferred. The reporting will not be selective.

Ahead-of-Its-Time Research and the [PERSON] Method Premise. The research character of the University has, since [PERSON], been distinguished by a willingness to undertake work whose immediate application is unclear and whose ultimate value depends on the patient unfolding of what later commentators have called the [PERSON] Method: the discipline of taking the halfbaked idea seriously, examining it in its half-baked state, and following it through the patient sequence of testing, recasting, and packaging by which [PERSON] produced, among other things, the wooden magnet, the boxed spark plug sparks, and the celebrated dehydrated water pills. The Plan extends the Method into a structured contemporary research posture.

Initiatives. 1. Establish the [PERSON] Method Fellowship: a ten-year research fellowship scheme for early-career researchers prepared to commit to work whose applications are unlikely to be visible within the term of the fellowship, with a published carrying capacity for the scheme set at two cohorts at any one time. 2. Convene the Wooden Magnet Working Group, named for one of [PERSON]’s signature investigations, charged with identifying research directions the University considers fifty years ahead of their time and protecting them against the funding cycle’s ordinary impatience. 3. Maintain and expand the [PERSON] Collections held at the Menzies Library, including the original sketches, working papers, and surviving prototypes, with the collection made progressively available for direct consultation by researchers across the [PLACE] region. Measures. 1. By 2031, the [PERSON] Method Fellowship will be funding two active cohorts, with the first ten-year cycle settled and an open call for the next. 2. The Wooden Magnet Working Group will have met quarterly from 2026 onwards, with minutes published in full. 3. By 2028, the [PERSON] Collections will have been fully digitised and made publicly accessible, with a published cataloguing standard shared with comparable national archives.

The world in 2026 The conditions in which [PLACE] higher education now operates are unlike those that shaped the institutional patterns of the last forty years. Four converging pressures bear most directly on a national university of [ORGANISATION]’s character. The first is sovereign. [PLACE] is being asked, with increasing seriousness across the political class and the public, to demonstrate that it has a sovereign research and education capability of a depth appropriate to a country of its standing. The Plan accordingly takes the [PERSON] tradition seriously as a substantive sovereign asset — not as a national-mythological curiosity but as a distinctive institutional disposition that no other [PLACE] university has structurally inherited. The second pressure is generational. The students entering the University in 2026 will be in the prime of their professional lives in 2046. The character of the formation the University offers them, across the long arc of their professional lives, is the substantive question to which the [PERSON] tradition has, since its inception, offered an unusually specific answer.

The third is sectoral. The settled assumptions of the previous decade can no longer be assumed. The University will not pretend that the adjustment is comfortable. The Plan articulates a posture appropriate to a research-intensive institution in a period in which the inherited financial settlements of the sector are under quiet pressure — a posture, the working group judged, for which the [PERSON] disposition is unusually well-fitted. The fourth pressure is the centenary itself. The University arrives at 2031 having had several decades in which it has, by general assessment, not always tended the [PERSON] tradition with the seriousness it warrants. The working group considers the period of this Plan a structural opportunity to address that under-tending, in anticipation of the centenary and of the institutional re-examination it will, properly, occasion. Read together, these four pressures ask the University to articulate its posture in terms that the [PERSON] tradition has long made available and that the institution has not, in recent strategic literature, made full use of. The Plan accordingly does so.

Foreword from the Vice-Chancellor [PERSON] Plan articulates the direction of the [ORGANISATION] across the period 2026 to 2031. The Plan is framed, throughout, by the institutional legacy of [PERSON], the University’s most consequential alumnus, whose centenary falls in the final year of the plan period. It is not the working group’s view, and it is not Council’s view, that institutional planning should reach unduly into the past. The view that has emerged across consultation, however, is that the [PERSON] tradition — often referred to in the University’s older literature simply as “the [PERSON] disposition” — continues to distinguish [ORGANISATION] from the institutions with which it is most often compared, and that the centenary year provides a structural occasion for the University to take fresh form around the disposition rather than merely commemorate its founder.

The disposition is well documented. [PERSON] characterised it, variously, as “the patient examination of the half-baked”, “the work of taking the unbaked seriously”, and, in the often-cited formulation from the 1948 notebook, “the discipline of recognising what is, in fact, packaged for use”. It produced, across the productive period of the 1920s and 1930s, the inventions for which he remains best known — the wooden magnet, the boxed spark plug sparks, the bottled spirit-level bubbles, the dehydrated water pills, the clockwork motor vehicle, and the around-the-corner hammer, among others — and it shaped the institutional culture of the University in ways that have continued, with admirable consistency, across the eight decades since. The Plan accordingly addresses the [PERSON] tradition as a substantive institutional commitment. It does so across four priorities — the [PERSON] legacy itself, the [PERSON] research method, the education of the [PERSON] posterity, and the stewardship of the [PERSON] Collections, Archives, and Spirit — each unpacked in the body of this document. We commend the Plan to the University community in the conviction that an institution which knows its tradition is an institution better placed to do its tradition’s continuing work. Vice-Chancellor and President

Vision By 2031, [ORGANISATION] will be a national university recognised — within the country, in its region, and across the global research community — as an institution that speaks in its own voice and means what it says. The University will have demonstrated, over the run of this Plan, that a serious national institution can take its own register seriously without sliding into parody, and that the country is the better served for the demonstration. The disciplines will have been tended with care; the partnerships will have been held in fair exchange; the federal capital will be a more recognisable seat of national scholarship in 2031 than it was in 2026.

Strategic pillars Fair Dinkum National Capability Context. The University was established to serve the country in the most direct sense. Across the previous decade, the language of that service has too often drifted away from the country’s own register and into something that could have been written anywhere. The Plan returns the University’s articulation of its national service to its own voice, and it does so structurally rather than cosmetically. Commitments. 1. Establish a National Voice Audit, published annually, examining the University’s external-facing strategic literature for register, voice, and clarity, with audit findings reported to Council. 2. Convene the Sovereign Capability Forum twice yearly, bringing the country’s policy community, the academy, and senior public service together around a small set of long-horizon questions of national capability. 3. Establish a Fair Dinkum Research Programme: a published list of research initiatives the University considers central to the country’s sovereign capability, with funding committed across the plan period and protected against ordinary funding-cycle reallocation. —9—

How we will deliver Governance arrangements for the Plan are deliberately conservative. Council retains its existing role as the ultimate steward of the University’s direction, and the ViceChancellor remains accountable to Council for delivery. Within that frame, three moves give the Plan effective traction. First, a standing Plan Delivery Committee, chaired by a Deputy Vice-Chancellor and reporting quarterly to Council, takes responsibility for the indicator set across all five priorities. Second, an annual Delivery Schedule, published in the first quarter of each year, sets out which indicators are due for full reporting in which quarter, with no indicator permitted to slip beyond the next quarterly review. Third, Council’s Audit and Risk Committee will, from 2027, treat indicator slippage on the same footing as financial sustainability. Annual reporting against the Plan will be published in full, including instances of indicator slippage and elements of the Plan that have not progressed at the pace this document anticipated. Conclusion The decade ahead will ask of [PLACE] universities a different kind of articulacy from the one the sector has spent the last forty years cultivating: the willingness to speak in the country’s own register and to mean what is said in it. The University’s wager, in this Plan, is that the institutions which continue to matter through the second half of this century will be those that have, in the second half of this decade, found the country’s voice and used it with the seriousness the moment requires. The work is patient and largely invisible from outside. Much of it is administrative rather than ceremonial. But the conditions on which a national university’s standing depends — voice, judgement, mateship, place, and a beaut set of bones — are not built in any other way. The University will tend them across the decade ahead.

Pillar 4: Stewardship and Institutional Renewal None of the above is possible without renewed institutional foundations. Over the plan period we will invest in the digital, physical, and human infrastructure on which [ORGANISATION] depends, and we will work toward an institutional culture in which every member of the community can do their best work.

Transformation initiatives • Modernise digital infrastructure, including a renewed approach to research data, a modernised teaching technology stack, and an institution-wide approach to artificial intelligence in education and research. • Refresh the campus precinct as a working environment fit for the next twenty-five years, with sustained investment in heritage assets, contemporary teaching spaces, and student amenities. • Build a culturally safe and structurally equitable working environment for all members of the [ORGANISATION] community, with clear measures of progress on representation, retention, and career advancement for staff and students from historically marginalised backgrounds. • Strengthen financial sustainability through diversified revenue, philanthropic capability uplift, and operational excellence in the university’s professional services functions.

Establish (2026) In the first year, we will put in place the governance, baselines, and foundational investments needed to deliver the plan. Each pillar will have a designated executive sponsor, a dedicated implementation team, and a published baseline against which progress will be measured. Foundational investments — in digital infrastructure, in flagship research initiatives, and in educational redesign — will commence.

Build (2027-2028) Through 2027 and 2028, the major investments and program changes set out in this plan will reach scale. New postgraduate programs will commence; flagship research initiatives will reach operational maturity; the campus precinct refresh will deliver its most visible early outcomes. The mid-period review will be undertaken in late 2028.

A distinctive position [ORGANISATION] sits in a particular position. We are [PLACE]’s national university, established by an Act of [PLACE] [ORGANISATION] with a charter to serve the nation. We are research-intensive at a scale and depth unmatched in the country. And we are home to research and teaching strengths — across the sciences, humanities, social sciences, and policy domains — that are genuinely globally distinctive. This position confers both opportunity and obligation. The opportunity is to make a contribution to the national effort that no other institution can. The obligation is to do so with the seriousness, the honesty, and the strategic clarity that the country deserves from its national university.

This vision is ambitious and focused. It reflects our distinctive mission, our particular institutional strengths, and the moment in which we find ourselves. It is grounded in eight decades of demonstrated capacity, and oriented toward the next.

Strategic pillars Pillar 1: Research Excellence and National Impact The defining feature of [ORGANISATION]’s research has always been its proximity to the questions that matter for [PLACE] and the wider world. Over the plan period we will sharpen that distinctiveness — focusing investment on mission-aligned research priorities, expanding our cross-disciplinary capability, and growing the research income on which the university’s future depends.

• Renew the university’s cross-disciplinary research capability, with a particular focus on the intersections of computing, the life sciences, and the humanities and social sciences. • Establish a national institute drawing together [ORGANISATION]’s distinctive strengths in equine genomics, livestock-systems modelling, and the environmental history of the [PLACE] pastoral economy — a vehicle through which the university’s research effort can be aligned with one of the country’s most enduring industrial and cultural traditions. • Strengthen the institutional supports for research integrity, research data, and the responsible use of artificial intelligence in research, ensuring that [ORGANISATION]’s research practice continues to set the standard for the sector.

Why this matters The [ORGANISATION] education has always been distinguished by its proximity to the research practice of the university and by its insistence on the slow, demanding work of disciplined thought. The decade ahead is one in which those distinctive qualities will matter more, not less, and one in which how we teach is at least as consequential as what we teach.

What we’ll do 1. Renew the undergraduate experience around inquiry, judgement, and the methodological traditions of the disciplines we teach, with a renewed emphasis on small-group teaching, seminar-based learning, and forms of classroom practice that prioritise sustained discussion over slide-driven delivery. 2. Embed a plurality of knowledges across the curriculum, including substantive engagement with [PLACE] methodologies and critical perspectives in disciplines that have historically marginalised them. 3. Lift HDR completions and reduce mean time-to-completion through redesigned candidature support, renewed supervisory frameworks, and more generous access to research training infrastructure.

Priority 3: Place, Partnership, and Reconciliation Universities flourish through their relationships with the communities they serve — and they fail when those relationships are characterised by extraction rather than partnership. Over the plan period we will deepen our engagement, take honest steps toward reconciliation, and build the conditions for belonging across the [ORGANISATION] community.

Why this matters [ORGANISATION] was founded to serve the nation, and the meaning of that service has continued to deepen across the university’s history. The decade ahead requires us to honour that founding intent through sustained, patient, honest partnership — with [PLACE] communities, with the [PLACE] public service, and with the publics that have always been the university’s reason for being.

How we’ll know 1. Operating margin sustained at or above five per cent across the plan period. 2. Net-zero direct emissions by 2035, with the campus precinct on a credible path to full operational sustainability. 3. By 2030, all major committee and executive decision papers at [ORGANISATION] will be circulated in advance as written briefs of no more than two pages, with slide decks retained only for ceremonial and external presentation use.

How we will deliver this plan The plan will be delivered in four overlapping phases across the period to 2031. The phases are sequential in emphasis but not in start — each priority will have activity under way from the first year of the plan.

Set in motion (2026) In the first year, we will put in place the governance, baselines, and foundational investments needed to deliver the plan. Each priority will have a designated executive sponsor, a dedicated implementation team, and a published baseline against which progress will be measured. Foundational investments — in flagship research initiatives, in educational redesign, and in the digital and physical infrastructure that supports them — will commence.

Deepen (2027-2028) Through 2027 and 2028, the major investments and program changes set out in this plan will reach scale. New postgraduate programs will commence; flagship research initiatives will reach operational maturity; the campus precinct refresh will deliver its most visible early outcomes. The mid-period review will be undertaken in late 2028.

Scale (2029-2030) Through 2029 and 2030, the focus will shift from build to scale — from new investment to sustained operational delivery. Programs will be tuned for outcomes; partnerships will deepen; success measures will be tracked publicly and acted on. The cultural and structural changes initiated in earlier phases will be expected to be visible in the lived experience of staff and students.

Strategic priorities The four priorities below structure the work of the plan period. Each is presented with a short premise, the transformation initiatives we will pursue, and the indicators by which we will track our progress.

From and to The plan represents a deliberate shift in the university’s posture across several dimensions. The transitions below are illustrative rather than exhaustive, and run through each of the priority areas that follow. From

Priority 1: Research Excellence and National Impact [ORGANISATION]’s research has always taken its character from the questions that matter for [PLACE] and the wider world. Over the plan period we will sharpen that distinctiveness — focusing investment on mission-aligned priorities, expanding our cross-disciplinary capability, and growing the research income on which the university’s future depends.

Why this matters A national university is judged in the long run by the substance of the research it produces and the difference that research makes to the country it serves. The decade ahead will reward institutions that concentrate their effort, sustain their depth, and remain honest about where they can lead.

2. Renew the university’s cross-disciplinary research capability, with a particular focus on the intersections of computing, the life sciences, and the humanities and social sciences, and the questions that sit between them. 3. Grow Category 1 and competitive research income substantially over the plan period, including through opportunities arising from successive [PLACE] research and capability instruments.

Priority 2: Education for the Decades Ahead The world our students will work in is being remade. Our educational programs will be redesigned around the dispositions, knowledges, and forms of inquiry that will matter most over the coming decades — with particular attention to critical perspectives, plurality of knowledges, and the capacity for sustained reasoning under uncertainty.

What we’ll do 1. Move beyond first-generation reconciliation work toward structural transformation, including a renewed [ORGANISATION], sustained investment in [PLACE]-led research, and a long-term commitment to truth telling about the university’s own history. 2. Deepen engagement with the [PLACE] public service, including through expansion of executive education, renewal of long-running partnerships with policy agencies, and a sustained programme of evidence-based contribution to national decision-making. 3. Build durable partnerships with civil-society organisations, primary industries, and the cultural sector, with at least 75 active strategic partnerships of national significance by 2031.

Priority 4: A Capable and Connected Institution None of the above is achievable without renewed institutional foundations. Over the plan period we will invest in the people, the systems, and the working culture on which the university depends — and we will commit to ways of working that match the seriousness of the academic mission they support.

Why this matters The quality of an institution’s work is shaped by the quality of its internal life. Universities make their best contribution when staff have the time, the systems, and the conditions to do work of substance — and when the institution’s own practices honour the kind of careful, deliberative reasoning the academic mission depends on.

What we’ll do 1. Modernise digital infrastructure, including a renewed approach to research data, a contemporary teaching technology stack, and an institution-wide approach to artificial intelligence in education, research, and administration. 2. Renew the conditions under which institutional decisions are made and communicated, with a renewed emphasis on written briefs, working papers, and

structured discussion in place of presentation-led decision-making, so that staff time is spent on argument rather than arrangement. 3. Build a culturally safe and structurally equitable working environment for all members of the [ORGANISATION] community, with clear measures of progress on representation, retention, and career advancement for staff and students from historically marginalised backgrounds.

Vice-Chancellor’s introduction This is the [ORGANISATION]’s strategic plan for the period 2026 to 2031. It sets out the directions the University will pursue over the next phase of its institutional life, and the choices we have made in setting them. The plan reflects our continuing commitment to research excellence, to the depth and seriousness of our educational programs, and to the partnerships through which a national university actually meets the country it serves. It also reflects the recognition that the work of a university is undertaken on a long horizon — shaped by problems we have only begun to see clearly, and by futures whose outlines remain to be drawn.

The directions in this plan have been informed by extensive consultation with our staff, students, alumni, partners, and Council. They are deliberate. They reflect choices made carefully, and they will require sustained effort to deliver. I want to thank the many members of our community who contributed to this plan, and in particular the staff, students, and external partners who pressed us to be both more honest and more ambitious. The result is, I believe, a plan worthy of the university we are working to become. I commend it to the [ORGANISATION] community. The work that follows is ours to do together. Vice-Chancellor and President

Executive summary [ORGANISATION] is an institution with a particular purpose: to serve the country through research, teaching, and engagement of the highest quality. This plan describes how we will sustain and renew that purpose over the period to 2031. The plan is structured around four strategic pillars: research excellence and discovery; a distinctive education; place, partnership, and reconciliation; and a connected and capable institution. Together they describe the university we are working to be. —5—

Deepen (2027-2028) Through 2027 and 2028, the major investments and program changes set out in this plan will reach scale. New programs will commence; flagship research initiatives will reach operational maturity; the campus precinct refresh will deliver its most visible early outcomes. The mid-period review will be undertaken in late 2028. — 14 —

Scale (2029-2030) Through 2029 and 2030, the focus will shift from build to scale — from new investment to sustained operational delivery. Programs will be tuned for outcomes; partnerships will deepen; success measures will be tracked publicly and acted on.

Sustain (2031) In 2031 we will assess what the plan has delivered, recalibrate where outcomes have not been met, and prepare the strategic direction for the period beyond. The 2031 review will be conducted with the same depth of consultation that produced this plan.

Accountability and review Council holds responsibility for oversight of this plan. The Vice-Chancellor and the executive are accountable to Council for its delivery. Each strategic pillar has a designated executive sponsor with operational responsibility for its implementation. The plan will be reported on annually to Council and to the broader university community. The annual report will describe progress against each success measure, will note decisions made in response to circumstances, and will be published on the university’s website. The report will be public, and it will be specific. A mid-period review will be conducted in late 2028 by an independent panel commissioned by Council. The review will assess progress, recommend adjustments where required, and be considered by Council before being implemented through the executive. The Audit and Risk Committee will oversee the controls associated with this plan. Material decisions affecting the strategic direction will be brought to Council for endorsement through the established governance arrangements. This plan is the university’s commitment to its community. Its implementation is our shared responsibility.

The decade ahead The decade to 2031 will demand much of [PLACE] and of the institutions on which the country relies. [ORGANISATION] will meet that demand with the seriousness, the honesty, and the strategic clarity that the moment requires. This plan describes the directions we will pursue and the choices we will make. Its delivery will require the sustained effort of every member of the [ORGANISATION] community — staff, students, alumni, and partners. We are confident in our trajectory, in our mission, and in the contribution that [ORGANISATION] will continue to make to the country, the region, and the world. The work begins now.

These pillars are interdependent. None can be fully realised in isolation. Together they describe a university that is ambitious, honest, durable, and recognisably [ORGANISATION]. The remainder of this document sets out, for each pillar, the transformation initiatives we will pursue and the success measures by which we will track our progress. It also describes our implementation approach and the governance arrangements that will hold us accountable to the directions set out here.

The world in 2026 Three transformations define the operating environment for [PLACE] universities in the years to 2031, and each interacts with the others in ways that demand a coordinated response. The first is technological. Advances in artificial intelligence, in computing infrastructure, and in adjacent fields are reshaping every research discipline and

every workforce. The capabilities that matter for our students — and for the country — are themselves in motion. Universities that fail to engage seriously with this transformation will find themselves diminished in both standing and contribution. The second is climatic. The decade ahead will see deepening pressure on natural systems and intensifying transitions across the energy, industrial, and agricultural systems on which our communities depend. Universities are central to navigating these transitions — through research, through the leadership they educate, and through the example they set in their own operations.

The third is geopolitical and cultural. [PLACE]’s place in the [PLACE] is being remade by demographic, economic, and intellectual currents that no longer flow along the familiar Atlantic axis. Across the region — and in the literary, scientific, and design cultures of partners such as the Republic of Korea, Japan, Singapore, and Indonesia — the questions of how technological societies should imagine their own futures, and how the public should be made a participant in that imagining, are being addressed with a seriousness from which [PLACE] universities have much to learn. A national university serious about its region must take that seriously too.

What we’ll do 1. Renew our partnerships with the federal public service, the parliament, and the cultural and scientific institutions of the national capital — recognising that [ORGANISATION]’s distinctive value to the country flows in significant part from its proximity to the institutions of national life. 2. Expand our structural research and education partnerships across the IndoPacific and with established [PLACE] peers, with a particular focus on long-term arrangements with [PLACE] and other Francophone institutions that complement our existing footprint and provide a durable counterweight in our partnership portfolio.

How we’ll know • By 2031, [ORGANISATION] will operate at least one permanently co-located joint research unit with a [PLACE] national research organisation, with reciprocal academic appointments and a published programme of work renewed at least biennially. • At least 50 active strategic partnerships with public-sector, industry, civil-society, and international research organisations. • [PLACE] student enrolments and [PLACE] staff representation to grow significantly across the plan period, supported by structural investment in pathways, supervision, and progression.

Priority 4: A Capable and Connected Institution Why this matters None of the above is possible without renewed institutional foundations. Executive summary This plan sets out five strategic priorities that will shape the work of the [ORGANISATION] through to 2031. Together they describe a coherent ambition: that [ORGANISATION] will become the country’s most consequential site for the integrated study of energies — historical, material, somatic, and planetary — and the most reliable institution for the cultivation of an energetic imagination across the disciplines on which [PLACE] public life depends.

The priorities are interlocking. None can be fully realised in isolation, and the plan is best read as a description of the university we are working to become over the plan period: attentive to the conditions on which institutional life rests, accountable for the energies it draws on and the energies it produces, and recognisably [ORGANISATION].

transformations are reshaping the operating environment for the university, and each interacts with the others in ways that demand a coordinated institutional response. The first is the maturation of the planetary energy transition. The decade ahead will see substantial decarbonisation of the country’s energy infrastructure, the recomposition of major industrial sectors, and the renewal of the cultural and political settings within which those shifts will be undertaken. Universities sit at the intersection of those shifts — as producers of the knowledge on which the transition depends, as educators of the workforces that will deliver it, and as institutions whose own operations are themselves part of the transition.

The second is the repositioning of the body within knowledge work. The postures, attentions, and conditions on which scholarship and teaching depend have, for a long time, been treated as external to the work itself. The plan period asks the institution to bring those conditions into the work — to recognise that the energetic conditions of academic and professional labour are themselves part of the institutional fabric, and that a research-intensive university that fails to attend to them will not sustain the conditions of its own future flourishing. The third is the rise of energetic accounting in institutional life. What was once an externality — the energy a building consumes, the energy a research programme draws on, the energy embodied in the materials of teaching — is increasingly an object of structured attention, with frameworks for measurement, reporting, and acting on what those frameworks reveal. A research-intensive university that takes that accounting seriously is one that the country can trust to lead the wider transition that comes with it.

[ORGANISATION] sits within this context with particular advantages and particular obligations. We are a research-intensive national university with depth across the disciplines on which the field of inquiry draws — the sciences, the engineering disciplines, the humanities, the social sciences, the creative arts — and a national charter to take seriously the questions on which the country’s public life depends. We are located in the country’s capital, deeply integrated with the institutions of national policy life, and within walking distance of the country’s foremost cultural and collecting institutions. The strategic choices in this plan reflect both that position and the work the period demands.

• Recognition of practice-led and embodied research as primary research outputs in the university’s formal promotion, workload, and reporting arrangements, adopted by 2027 and sustained throughout the plan period. • Sustained improvement in staff and student wellbeing indicators across the plan period, with particular attention to the conditions of energetic sustainability in the academic working week.

Looking ahead The decade ahead will not be a quiet one. And we are home to research and teaching strengths — across the sciences, humanities, social sciences, and policy domains — that are genuinely globally distinctive. This position confers both opportunity and obligation. The opportunity is to make a contribution to the national effort that no other institution can. The obligation is to do so with the seriousness, the independence, and the strategic clarity that the country deserves from its national university. This plan describes how we will meet that obligation over the years to 2031.

A vision for [ORGANISATION] in 2031 By 2031, the [ORGANISATION] will be the world-leading university for the study of [PLACE] and its place in the [PLACE] — recognised globally for the depth of its research, the quality of its educational programs, and the durability of its contribution to national and regional life. This vision is ambitious and focused. It reflects our distinctive mission, our particular institutional strengths, and the moment in which we find ourselves. It is grounded in eight decades of demonstrated capacity and oriented toward the next.

Strategic pillars Pillar 1: Discovery for the Nation [ORGANISATION]’s research has always been distinguished by purpose, scale, and proximity to the questions that matter for [PLACE]. Over the plan period we will sharpen that distinctiveness — concentrating investment in mission-aligned research priorities, expanding cross-disciplinary capability, and growing our research income through programs that deliver national impact.

Transformation initiatives • Strengthen mission-aligned research in critical and emerging technologies, with sustained investment in three to five flagship programs. • Build the country’s most ambitious cross-disciplinary research initiatives at the intersections of computing, the life sciences, and the humanities. • Grow Category 1 research income through nationally significant programs, with a particular focus on opportunities arising from the National Reconstruction Fund and successor instruments. • Expand sovereign research infrastructure — high-performance computing, secure facilities, and specialist instruments — across the campus and partner sites.

Pillar 2: Education for a Changing World The world our students will work in is being remade. Our educational programs will be redesigned around the dispositions and capabilities that will matter most over the coming decades: deep disciplinary judgement, comfort with technical complexity, and the capacity for inquiry under uncertainty.

Transformation initiatives • Renew the undergraduate experience around inquiry, judgement, and futures literacy, with substantive curriculum redesign across all colleges by 2028. • Build new postgraduate programs in [PLACE] affairs, advanced computing, and public policy, drawing on [ORGANISATION]’s distinctive depth in each area. • Embed work-integrated and placement-based learning across all faculties, with particular emphasis on partnerships with the federal public service and key industries. • Lift HDR completions and reduce mean time-to-completion through redesigned candidature support and renewed supervisory frameworks.

Pillar 3: Engagement and Reconciliation Universities flourish through their relationships with the communities they serve. Over the plan period we will deepen our partnership with [PLACE] communities, sustain our engagement with the federal public service, and build durable industry partnerships in the sectors that matter most for [PLACE]’s future.

Build (2027-2028) Through 2027 and 2028, the major investments and program changes set out in this plan will reach scale. New postgraduate programs will commence; flagship research initiatives will reach operational maturity; the campus precinct refresh will deliver its most visible early outcomes. The mid-period review will be undertaken in late 2028.

Embed (2029-2030) Through 2029 and 2030, the focus will shift from build to embed — from new investment to sustained operational delivery. Programs will be tuned for outcomes; partnerships will deepen; success measures will be tracked publicly and acted on.

Renew (2031) In 2031 we will assess what the plan has delivered, recalibrate where outcomes have not been met, and prepare the strategic direction for the period beyond. The 2031 review will be conducted with the same depth of consultation that produced this plan.

Governance and accountability Council holds responsibility for oversight of this plan. The Vice-Chancellor and the executive are accountable to Council for its delivery. Each strategic pillar has a designated executive sponsor with operational responsibility for its implementation. The plan will be reported on annually to Council and to the broader university community. The annual report will describe progress against each success measure, will highlight decisions made in response to circumstances, and will be published on the university’s website.

A mid-period review will be conducted in late 2028 by an independent panel commissioned by Council. The review will assess progress, will recommend adjustments where required, and will be considered by Council before being implemented through the executive. The Audit and Risk Committee will oversee the controls associated with this plan. Material decisions affecting the strategic direction will be brought to Council for endorsement through the established governance arrangements. This plan is the university’s commitment to its community. Its implementation is our shared responsibility.

Our values The values below emerged through consultation as the dispositions that participants returned to most often when describing the kind of institution the Plan is asking [ORGANISATION] to become. The accompanying glosses preserve the language in which the values were spoken. Set — The conditions of the encounter shape the encounter. The University attends to the mindset, intention, and preparation with which it approaches its work. Setting — The container is part of the work. The University attends to the physical, relational, and temporal conditions in which inquiry is held. Integration — Without integration, the insight disperses. The University takes seriously the slow work of embedding what its inquiry has surfaced. Dose — The right dose for the right purpose. The University calibrates the intensity of its interventions to the durable change they intend to produce. Container — That which holds, holds itself. The University maintains the structural conditions that allow significant work to be undertaken without dispersal.

Four converging pressures bear most directly on a national university of [ORGANISATION]’s character, each of which informs the framing of this Plan. The first is the intensity of the operating environment itself. Universities are being asked to undertake research and teaching on questions of increasing magnitude and pace — climate, sovereign capability, the rapid development of artificial intelligence, intergenerational equity — under conditions in which the institutional container of the previous decade was not designed to hold them. Integration Practice: From Insight to Embedded Outcome Premise. The literature is consistent in finding that an episode without integration produces, over time, no durable change in the experiencer. The same is true of an institution: a research finding without integration produces no durable change in the discipline; a strategic insight without integration produces no durable change in the institution. The Plan accordingly invests in integration practice as a substantive institutional commitment, not as a post-experience tidying-up exercise. Initiatives. 1. Establish Integration [PLACE] Rooms in every College: physical spaces dedicated to the slow integration of significant research and teaching, with reading lists maintained and updated by the Integration Practice Committee and access available to staff and students across the University. 2. Convene quarterly Integration Circles, structured to a formal protocol and attended by representatives from across every College, with the purpose of integrating the period’s significant research and institutional findings into the working understanding of the company. 3. Embed Integration Weeks twice yearly in the academic and operational calendar, during which routine reporting is suspended and the institution practises the disciplines of post-experience integration. Measures. 1. By 2031, Integration [PLACE] Rooms will be in operation in every College, with annual reporting of usage to the Deputy Vice-Chancellor (Academic). 2. Accountability and review Governance arrangements for the Plan are deliberately conservative. Council retains its existing role as the ultimate steward of the University’s direction, and the ViceChancellor remains accountable to Council for delivery. Within that frame, three governance moves give the Plan effective traction. First, a standing Set & Setting Committee, chaired by a Deputy Vice-Chancellor and reporting quarterly to Council, takes responsibility for the indicator set across all four priorities and for surfacing slippage in any of them. Second, an Accountability and Review schedule, published annually, sets out which indicators are due for full reporting in which quarter, with no indicator permitted to slip beyond the next quarterly review cycle. Third, Council’s Audit and Risk Committee will, from 2027, treat the Set & Setting Index on the same footing as financial sustainability. Annual reporting against the Plan will be published in full, including instances of indicator slippage, any Heroic Dose Programme item whose Post-Dose Integration has not been completed within the quarter following completion, and any element of the Plan that has not progressed at the pace this document anticipated. The reporting will not be selective. The University takes the view that the credibility of an institutional posture grounded in integration practice depends, in the first instance, on the willingness to publish the periods in which integration has not, in fact, occurred.

Glossary This Plan uses a small set of terms drawn from the contemporary discipline of set, setting, and integration practice. The terms are defined here as they are used across the document. Container. The structural arrangements — physical, relational, temporal, and procedural — within which a significant institutional experience is held. In the Plan, the term denotes the institutional analogue of the literature’s reference to the conditions of safe holding. Heroic dose. A major institutional commitment of sufficient intensity to require structural container arrangements distinct from those of ordinary institutional work. In the Plan, the term denotes items in the Heroic Dose Programme.

Vice-Chancellor’s introduction This Strategic Plan articulates the direction of the [ORGANISATION] across the period 2026 to 2031. The Plan does so through a framing the working group settled on early in the drafting process and held throughout: that an institution of [ORGANISATION]’s complexity is best understood as a production — a long-running production with an overture, character arcs, ensemble numbers, and a closing standing ovation that the institution intends to earn rather than expect. The framing is not metaphorical decoration. A long-running production has the same operational characteristics as a long-running national institution. It requires a script that the company believes in. It requires rehearsal time that the schedule must protect. It requires a producer’s discipline about which numbers are working and which are not. And it requires an honest assessment, at the end of each season, of where the production is on its run.

This Plan describes how the University will run its production over the next five years. It describes the kinds of standing-ovation moments — the showstoppers, the eleven o’clock numbers, the encores — that the institution intends to earn, and it describes the kinds of supporting work, often invisible from the stalls, that those moments require. We commend the Plan to the University community in the conviction that a national university which understands its own staging is a national university more likely to do its work well. Vice-Chancellor and President

The fourth pressure is epistemic. The sector has drifted, over the previous decade, toward measures of academic productivity that reward throughput over the slower forms of work on which a research university’s reputation is in fact built. The applause that a university most needs is not the kind that follows a flashy opening; it is the kind that follows the eleven o’clock number — the moment, late in the run, when the audience recognises the depth of what the company has been doing all along. Read together, these four pressures ask the University to articulate its purpose with the seriousness of a production that intends a long run, rather than the seriousness of a production hoping to survive its previews. Foundations for a Sovereign Practice Why this matters. The practice of new instrument-making depends on a constellation of capabilities — fabrication, computing, archive, acoustical, professional — without which the most ambitious ideas remain notional. The plan period asks [ORGANISATION] to underwrite those capabilities for the country, in the same way the country has historically underwritten the foundational capabilities on which national research and cultural life depend. What we’ll do. 1. Consolidate [ORGANISATION]’s instrumental-practice infrastructure into a coordinated precinct, including a fabrication suite, a controlled- acoustic facility, a public facing performance space, a climate- controlled instrument archive, and the digital infrastructure required to sustain them across decades.

2. Establish the [ORGANISATION] Instrumental Practice Archive as a permanent, climatecontrolled, publicly accessible repository for instruments designed and built at [ORGANISATION] and by partner institutions, with curatorial and conservation arrangements appropriate to objects intended to remain playable. 3. Renew the professional support arrangements — workshop staff, archive curators, programme administrators, technicians, and safety officers — without which the foundational capabilities cannot be sustained, with workforce-capability and wellbeing measures tracked publicly across the plan period.

How we’ll know. • The [ORGANISATION] Instrumental Practice Archive operational and open to the public by 2029, with curatorial standards and a published acquisition policy adopted by Council and a published custodial register sustained from opening. • A precinct-wide fabrication and acoustic capability operating at sustained scale from 2028, with audited access, equity-of-access measures, and a published utilisation framework reported on annually. • Renewed professional-staff arrangements in place by 2027, with workforcecapability and wellbeing indicators in the top quartile of comparable [PLACE] research-intensive universities across the plan period.

A message from the ViceChancellor This Strategic Plan articulates the direction of the [ORGANISATION] across the period 2026 to 2031. The Plan is also, by deliberate choice, a document that takes more care than is usual with the language in which institutional intent is set down. There is a saying that returned to the working group across many drafts: one cannot polish a river. The Plan does not aspire to polish what was already a river. It does aspire to follow that river with attentiveness. What we have learned, across consultation with staff, students, alumni, partners, and [PLACE] colleagues, is that a national university’s voice is one of its most durable assets — and one of the most easily flattened by the standard registers of strategic planning. We have accordingly attempted to speak in our own voice across these pages, even where that voice gathers its strength from sources outside the contemporary sectoral idiom.

The blacksmith’s hammer asks no questions of the anvil: this Plan, similarly, makes its commitments without apologising for the unusual grammar in which it sometimes makes them. Across the five priorities that follow, the substance is recognisably the substance of a national university plan — research, education, place, partnership, and institutional capability. The framing is, in moments, less recognisable. We commend the Plan to the community in the conviction that the goat does not weep at the herder’s wedding — that the relations which sustain an institution over a long period are worth tending with whatever language carries them best. Vice-Chancellor and President

A second consideration is intergenerational. Vision By 2031, [ORGANISATION] will be the [PLACE] institution most fluent in the crossings between analogue and digital practice. The Hybrid Substrate Premise. The most productive contemporary scholarship operates at the crossing between analogue and digital substrates, not entirely on either side of it. Foreword from the Vice-Chancellor [ORGANISATION] has always operated across the boundary between analogue and digital practice. The lab bench has long sat beside the model; the manuscript beside the database; the field notebook beside the corpus; the oscilloscope beside the laptop; the print and the screen. For most of the University’s history, these have been treated as adjacent practices that occasionally exchanged material. This Strategic Plan sets out the University’s settings for the period 2026 to 2031, during which we will treat the crossings themselves — the moments of translation between analogue and digital substrates — as primary scholarly material.

The decade ahead will see continued pressure across the higher-education sector to migrate further and faster onto digital substrates. [ORGANISATION]’s posture will be neither to accelerate that movement nor to resist it, but to articulate a third position: that the most distinctive contemporary scholarship operates at the crossing between analogue and digital practice, and that the institutional capacity to hold both seriously is a capacity worth investing in for its own sake. The Plan that follows is the University’s commitment to that posture. We have organised the work around five strategic priorities, a delivery arc across four phases, and a governance posture that places translation across the crossing at the centre of the institution’s methodological accountability. The Plan draws on every college and every professional cohort. I commend it to the University community. Vice-Chancellor and President

Executive summary In the period to 2031, [ORGANISATION] will become the [PLACE] institution most fluent in the crossings between analogue and digital practice. Strategic context The decade now under way has substantially advanced the digital migration of [PLACE] higher education. Teaching materials are now overwhelmingly assembled, distributed, and assessed through digital platforms; research workflows in many disciplines are predominantly computational; institutional records, including those that once defined the university’s relationship to its own history, exist in digital form. —6—

The migration has also, in places, produced losses that the sector has been slower to acknowledge. Material reasoning — the felt understanding of the medium that older traditions of inquiry built into their methodologies — has weakened in disciplines that have moved most decisively onto digital substrates. Computational literacy, conversely, has remained uneven in disciplines whose practice involves the daily use of computational tools that are nonetheless treated as background infrastructure rather than as scholarship. The translation work that mediates the crossing — the digitisation of physical archives, the printing of generative work, the encoding of field instruments, the materialisation of simulations — is conducted across the sector by talented practitioners who are rarely supported in articulating their craft as scholarly work in its own right. For [ORGANISATION], these developments cut across the four colleges. In the sciences, the computational and material dimensions of inquiry are increasingly entangled in instrument-led work that resists clean assignment to one side or the other. In the humanities and social sciences, the digital methods now central to many lines of inquiry sit alongside material traditions whose methodological commitments remain consequential. In the [ORGANISATION], the discipline of computing is itself the site at which the question of how computational systems are materially conditioned is most acutely posed. In the [ORGANISATION], the analogue and digital dimensions of clinical and laboratory work are knotted together in ways that the methodological vocabulary of any single tradition struggles to articulate.

Translation, Provenance, and the Crossing Premise. The work of moving between analogue and digital substrates — the digitisation of a physical archive, the printing of a generative work, the encoding of a field instrument, the materialisation of a simulation — is itself scholarship that the University has rarely articulated as such. [ORGANISATION] will treat translation across the crossing as a primary scholarly object. Initiatives. 1. The world in 2026 A demanding decade The operating environment for [PLACE] universities over the period to 2031 is defined by three deep and interacting transformations. Each calls for sustained, coordinated institutional response; together they shape the strategic context in which this plan will be delivered. The first is geopolitical and economic. The [PLACE] is the most strategically significant region in the world, and the country’s prosperity, security, and standing depend on the quality of the knowledge and capability we bring to bear on it. Universities have a direct role to play here — through research that informs national decision-making, through the people they educate, and through the depth of regional expertise they sustain over the long term. The second is technological. Advances in artificial intelligence, in computing infrastructure, and in adjacent fields are reshaping every research discipline and every workforce. The capabilities our students will need — and that the country will rely on — are themselves in motion. Universities that fail to engage seriously with this transformation will find themselves quietly diminished.

The third is closer to the texture of academic and policy work itself. Across government and industry, decision-makers are increasingly preparing for futures that cannot be inferred from past data alone, and the methods by which judgement is rehearsed — structured exercises, scenario-based deliberation, the patient practice of difficult choices in low-stakes settings before they arrive in high-stakes ones — have returned to the centre of serious institutional life. Universities that take this shift seriously will be unusually well placed to contribute; those that mistake it for a presentational fashion will be left behind.

Our agenda Institutional Assurance and Foresight Why this matters The University has, in effect, run four plans at once for as long as it has had four kinds of unit reporting on their own progress in their own terms and on their own schedule. That approach served the institution reasonably well when its scale was smaller and its obligations to funders and government were lighter; it no longer does. Institutional Assurance and Foresight exists to give the University a single, continuously current account of how its strategic commitments — across every pillar, including this one — are actually tracking, and to direct attention and resourcing toward whichever commitment needs it most in a given quarter, rather than waiting for the commitment to fail publicly first. That redirection is itself now a standing feature of how the University is run, not a one-off correction — a scale of change that, we recognise, asks more of every pillar lead than any previous planning cycle has. External advice on how such a system should be built, and how it should be received by the people it measures, is drawn from the University’s own research capability: Dr [PERSON], Senior Research Fellow in the [ORGANISATION], whose fieldwork traces how planning is actually practised inside institutions, will advise the program on how delivery-confidence scoring lands with the units it covers, and on where the architecture’s design should bend to fit the practice rather than the reverse.

What we’ll do 1. Establish an AI-governance early-warning system spanning every pillar and budget line of this plan, reporting a live delivery-confidence score to the Council and the Executive. 2. Bring each pillar’s reporting into a single assurance architecture, replacing the separate reporting rhythms each pillar has historically kept. 3. Direct a standing share of pillar funding, reallocated quarterly, toward whichever pillar’s delivery-confidence score is lowest in that quarter — including, where the data supports it, this pillar’s own build-out.
